verdict_reasoning: No objection survived against the change on master, where it is a small refactoring that the listed committer supports. The one surviving objection, maintenance-fit-1, concerns the proposed PG 19 backpatch: the patch changes an exported signature in ipc.h and adds a value in the middle of an enum, and the thread names no future backpatch that needs it. Targeting master only resolves it, and that choice belongs to the committer.

brief.title: Compute shared memory size once at startup and add SRS_SIZED state
brief.problem: During normal startup the server calls CalculateShmemSize() twice, once in InitializeShmemGUCs() and once in CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores(). The author wants to drop the duplicate calculation and make sure GUC reporting and segment creation use the same size. The audience is server developers who maintain this code.
brief.proposed_design: Startup code calls CalculateShmemSize() once, after ShmemCallRequestCallbacks(), and passes the result to InitializeShmemGUCs() and CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores(). A new shmem_request_state value, SRS_SIZED, sits between SRS_REQUESTING and SRS_INITIALIZING, so the server cannot register new requests after sizing. An Assert catches a second sizing call in the same cycle, and ResetShmemAllocator() resets the state on crash restart.
user_visible_surface: C API: CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() now takes a Size argument.
C API: InitializeShmemGUCs() receives the calculated size from its caller.
C API: new SRS_SIZED value in shmem_request_state; extensions that register shared memory requests after sizing are rejected.
author_claims: Removes a duplicate shared memory size calculation during startup.
GUC reporting and segment creation use the same calculated size.
No request can be registered after sizing, so initialization allocates exactly what was sized.
An Assert is enough for repeated sizing calls because this is an internal lifecycle invariant.
Worth backpatching to PG 19 to reduce conflicts in later backpatches, though it is not a bug fix.
brief.thread_state: Nathan Bossart (listed committer), Srinath Reddy Sadipiralla and Xuneng Zhou support the patch, and the author squashed both parts into one patch after review. Xuneng Zhou would prefer an ERROR to an Assert, and nobody has decided on the PG 19 backpatch.
unclear: The material does not say whether any extension or core path registers shared memory requests after sizing today and would now fail.
The patch does not say how postgres -C reaches runtime-computed GUCs under the new call order.
The material does not show how the EXEC_BACKEND and late allocation paths skip SRS_SIZED.
The thread has no justification for backpatching a refactoring to PG 19 beyond easier future backpatches.
Nobody tested restart_after_crash in a non-assert build, where the Assert does not run.

objections.title: Backpatching to PG 19 changes exported API and startup behaviour in a stable branch
objections.failure_scenario: A packager ships a PG 19 minor release with this patch. An extension built against an earlier 19.x minor that calls CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() now passes the wrong arguments. A library that registers a shared memory request between sizing and initialization now fails at server start. The user finds out only after the minor update.
objections.argument: The patch changes the signature of an exported function and adds an enum value in the middle of shmem_request_state. It also makes a previously accepted request timing fail at runtime. The only reason given for PG 19 is fewer conflicts in later backpatches (message #1, message #3), and the author says it is not a bug fix. A committer would likely ask for master only, since stable branches do not usually take refactorings that change exported symbols.
objections.author_must_show: Which concrete future backpatch would conflict without this change, and can the PG 19 version keep the old function signature and enum order?

critic.reasoning: The patch changes an exported signature in ipc.h, and the thread gives no concrete future backpatch that justifies this in PG 19. The late-request failure is unshown, but the ABI point stands alone, and targeting master only resolves it.

refuted.title: Backpatching to PG 19 changes C signatures and startup rules in a minor release
refuted.failure_scenario: A packager ships 19.x with this change. An extension that registers a shared memory request after sizing used to start because the segment had slack, and now the server refuses to start after a minor update. Any out-of-tree caller of CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() or InitializeShmemGUCs() also stops compiling against the new minor release.
refuted.argument: Message #1 and message #3 propose PG 19 only to reduce later backpatch conflicts, and the commit message calls this a refactoring that is not a bug fix. The patch changes two exported function signatures and adds a state that rejects requests which were accepted before. On master, extension authors expect such changes at a major release. In a stable branch they get a startup failure from a minor update, and the thread does not weigh that cost against fewer merge conflicts.
refuted.author_must_show: Which later backpatch is expected to conflict, and why is that worth a signature change and a new startup rejection in PG 19 minor releases?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1. Message #1, not the commit message, says the change is not a bug fix, and no extension is shown to register requests after sizing.

refuted.title: Backpatch to PG 19 changes exported function signature and request rules
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension or fork built against PG 19 calls CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() with no argument, or registers a shared memory request after sizing. After a minor update that carries this patch, the call no longer matches the binary's signature, or the request is rejected at startup. The user finds out when the server fails to start after a routine minor upgrade.
refuted.argument: Message #1 proposes PG 19 only to ease future backpatches, and message #3 agrees, but nobody has decided. The patch changes the signature of CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() in ipc.h. It also makes a request window that used to be accepted into an error, because the state stayed SRS_REQUESTING until initialization began. On a stable branch, a refactoring is usually not allowed to change an exported symbol or tighten runtime rules.
refuted.author_must_show: For PG 19, can the patch keep the old CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores() signature and request behaviour, or should it target master only?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same point about the signature change and the stricter request rule in PG 19 and also covers the enum order.

refuted.title: Backpatch to PG 19 moves extension risk into a stable branch
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension registers a shared memory request after sizing, or calls CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores(). After a PG 19 minor update, the request is rejected or the build breaks on the new Size argument. The extension's users find out when the server fails to start after a routine minor upgrade.
refuted.argument: Message #1 offers the PG 19 backpatch only to reduce conflicts in later backpatches, and calls it not a bug fix. Message #3 agrees, and nobody else has decided. The gain goes to developers who backpatch. The cost falls on extension users of a released branch, where the new SRS_SIZED check and the signature change are behaviour and API changes. Neither message #1 nor message #3 lists a concrete planned backpatch that needs this.
refuted.author_must_show: Which planned PG 19 backpatches would conflict without this change, and can you show that no known extension registers shared memory requests after sizing?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1. The who-pays framing adds no new fact beyond the PG 19 signature change and the stricter request rule.

committability.owner_note: Nathan Bossart is listed as committer on the CommitFest entry, reviewed the patch in message #2, and says there that the double call came from his own earlier work.
committability.liability: The owner signs for startup and crash-restart sizing of shared memory on all platforms, including EXEC_BACKEND, and for any extension that the new SRS_SIZED check rejects. If the patch goes to PG 19, the owner also signs for the ABI change in a stable branch.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a revised patch in message #7 that squashes both parts after review, and offered in message #1 to update the patch further.

priority.reason: The patch is about 9 KB across six startup and shared memory files, benefits developers who maintain this code, and has a committer engaged. The PG 19 backpatch is the only open point, and it can be dropped without changing the master patch.

precedents_retrieved.title: WIP: Track relation size in shared memory
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pool of SMgrSharedRelation objects in shared memory that holds the authoritative size of each recently extended or truncated relation until the file is fsync'd, so backends stop calling lseek(SEEK_END). The aim was fewer system calls and correct sizes on filesystems such as NFS that can shrink files asynchronously; an earlier recovery-only size cache from the same thread was committed separately (c5315f4f).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stayed at prototype stage. The author said a main piece was missing: a background process to clean dirty SR objects, so that foreground processes rarely block on fsync during eviction. Review comments from Buzhen, Andres and later Anastasia Lubennikova were still open, for example on CREATE DATABASE, which bypasses smgr, and on temporary relations. The visible messages show no reply after the July 2021 review before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The main thing being: how can we clean these objects in the background?  That question being unanswered, there is a 0% chance of committing this in PostgreSQL 14.

precedents_retrieved.title: Shared-memory based stats collector
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the file-based stats collector with statistics kept in dynamic shared memory (dshash), so backends read stats without a stats file written by a separate process. The stats collector process goes away, and per-kind stats code moves into new files under utils/activity.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reworked the patch in spring 2021 and judged it not committable for v14, citing weak test coverage, the need for architectural review and performance testing, an unresolved case where stats for dropped functions can be revived, and many open FIXMEs. A rebase then stalled on a new issue with partitioned tables. No new version was posted after July 2021, so the CommitFest manager marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately I think
that, while it has gotten a lot closer, it's still about a week's worth of
work away from being committable.

precedents_retrieved.title: Function to track shmem reinit time
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Tomas Vondra, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a function pg_shmem_init_time() that returns when shared memory was last initialized or reinitialized, so monitoring tools can detect crash restarts under restart_after_crash without parsing the server log. A second small patch removes dead shared memory reinit code and fixes comments in postmaster.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers doubted the premise. Tom Lane argued that the time of the last crash says little about how often crashes happen, and that improving the log would matter more. Tomas Vondra showed that comparing the value to pg_postmaster_start_time fails because the two come from separate timestamp calls, and Peter Eisentraut objected to a name that exposes shared memory internals. The patch also stopped applying after commit fd1a421fe, and the entry was returned with feedback with no new version posted; Robert Haas later spoke in favour and suggested an out-of-core extension.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think that if we're to do anything in this area,
improving the usefulness of the log would be more important than
providing the proposed function.

precedents_retrieved.title: Request for votes: Should we remove -Wdeclaration-after-statement?
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Robert Haas, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The proposal removes the -Wdeclaration-after-statement compiler warning so new code can declare variables at first use instead of at the top of a block. The author argued that the C89 reason is gone now that all supported branches require C99, and did not propose rewriting existing code.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The vote showed consensus against the change, and Robert Haas marked the entry rejected on that basis. Opponents wanted to keep one consistent declaration style and did not want declaration placement to become a matter of personal taste. They expected that, without the warning, different committers would place declarations in different ways. Some votes supported the change, including Noah Misch, who cited fewer back-patch merge conflicts.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The fact that all of our code uses a consistent style is awfully nice, too.

precedents_retrieved.title: Be strict when request to flush past end of WAL in WaitXLogInsertionsToFinish
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first proposed raising the "request to flush past end of generated WAL" message in WaitXLogInsertionsToFinish() from LOG to PANIC. It later moved to a patch that makes XLogBackgroundFlush() honor the adjusted (clamped) return value instead of discarding it, plus a TAP test that reproduces the header-only flush that broke replay on a standby.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was not rejected on its merits. Bharath Rupireddy created commitfest entry #7294 without knowing the author had already registered #7252 for the same thread. The author asked for #7294 to be withdrawn so the history stays in one entry, and it was withdrawn on the same day.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Could you withdraw #7294 so we don't split the history between two entries?

precedents_retrieved.title: Function to track shmem reinit time
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Peter Eisentraut, Tomas Vondra
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a function pg_shmem_init_time() that returns when shared memory was last initialized or reinitialized, so monitoring tools can detect crash restarts without parsing logs. A second patch removes dead shared memory reinit code in postmaster.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the function exposes an implementation detail that may change, and that frequent crashes should be fixed, not measured. Earlier, Peter Eisentraut objected to the shmem-based name, and Tomas Vondra argued that comparing with pg_postmaster_start_time does not reliably detect restarts. Robert Haas and Alexander Korotkov supported it, and David Steele returned the entry because the discussion stayed at an impasse.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
(1) it's exposing an implementation detail that clients should not be
concerned with, and that we might change in future.

This reverts commit ee1e5662d8d8330726eaef7d3110cb7add24d058, as well as

precedents_retrieved.title: XLog size reductions: Reduced XLog record header size
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset makes the WAL record header variable-length, which shrinks it to 14-21 bytes, with about 4-5% less WAL estimated for pgbench. It varlength-encodes the record length, gives rmgrs their own info byte, includes the XID only when the record asks for it with XLOG_INCLUDE_XID, and adds an invalid rmgr ID 0 used to detect the end of WAL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after review. Michael Paquier objected to the opt-in XLOG_INCLUDE_XID interface and questioned the use of rmgr ID 0 as an end-of-WAL marker. Pavel Borisov then asked for benchmarks showing the gain was large enough, the benchmarking was still a todo, and a reminder from Andrey M. Borodin in April 2024 got no visible reply before the entry was returned.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But at the second round, some doubt arises on whether this long
patchset indeed introduces enough performance gain?

precedents_retrieved.title: Simplify standby state machine a bit in WaitForWALToBecomeAvailable()
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes the standby state machine in WaitForWALToBecomeAvailable() set currentSource to XLOG_FROM_PG_WAL after a failed archive read, so XLogFileReadAnyTLI() no longer falls back to pg_wal itself. The current source is then passed to XLogFileReadAnyTLI() directly, without the XLOG_FROM_ANY special case.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier showed that the patch undoes commit 4d894b41. On HEAD, XLogFileReadAnyTLI() checks the archive and then pg_wal for each timeline in turn. With the patch it checks the archive for all timelines and only then pg_wal, so a segment with a higher TLI in pg_wal is no longer preferred. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And this patch basically undoes that, meaning that we would basically look at the archives first for all the expected TLIs, but only if no files were found in pg_wal/.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the corpus search returned no earlier attempt at this idea. In the thread, message #2 has the committer say the double call is his own earlier choice, and nobody points to a rejected discussion of this refactoring.

On master the change is internal and does not touch SQL, GUC semantics, pg_dump or psql. The thread keeps the postgres -C path separate (message #1), so I see no user-facing compatibility objection for master.
The patch touches only shared memory sizing at startup. It changes no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog or wire protocol, so the only concern from this angle is the proposed PG 19 backpatch.

The patch changes when the postmaster sizes shared memory and adds an internal state. It adds no new privilege and no new user-facing interface. It also gives no non-superuser a new way to see data or use resources. Shared memory requests come only from core and from preloaded libraries that a superuser configured, so the new SRS_SIZED check gives no unprivileged user a path to escalation or denial of service.

For master, I found no maintenance or fit objection. The change is a small refactoring of existing startup code, it tightens an existing state machine, adds no per-query cost, and the committer who wrote the original code has engaged and taken the entry.

This is an internal refactoring of startup sizing. No existing feature, extension or hook already removes the duplicate CalculateShmemSize() call. SRS_SIZED extends the existing shmem_request_state machine and adds no second mechanism, so this angle has nothing to raise.

For master the demand question does not apply. This is an internal cleanup that Nathan Bossart supports as the listed committer, and it has no user-facing cost. Only the PG 19 backpatch lacks a stated need.
